one_liner: Code-generating C++ ORM for MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server; its 2x-over-Dapper claim compares different databases.
what_it_does: ODB persists ordinary C++ classes to a relational database. You mark classes and members with #pragma db, and the ODB compiler (a GCC plugin) reads those headers and generates -odb.hxx/-odb.cxx files with the column mapping, SQL statements and optional schema. At run time you link libodb plus one libodb-<database> runtime and call database::persist/load/update/erase/query inside transactions, with sessions (an object cache), views, prepared queries, schema evolution and Boost/Qt profiles. It is a full ORM with its own API and build step, not a thin client and not a drop-in for Dapper or a raw database API.
how_it_is_fast: The mapping is generated at build time, so there is no runtime reflection or string-keyed column lookup. Generated per-class bind buffers go straight into each database's native C API: the MySQL runtime uses the binary prepared-statement protocol (mysql_stmt_prepare, mysql_stmt_bind_param/bind_result, mysql_stmt_fetch), and SQLite uses sqlite3_bind/step. Prepared statements are built once per connection and kept in a statement_cache keyed by type_info, connections are pooled, and an optional session cache avoids reloading objects already in memory. Explicit prepared queries, bulk persist/update/erase (Oracle and SQL Server only) and, since 2.6.0, direct loading of containers of object pointers in one SELECT (to avoid the N+1 problem) reduce round trips further.
when_to_use: C++ applications that store typed domain objects (with relationships, inheritance, containers) in MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite and want the mapping code generated instead of hand-written binding code
Code that must run against several databases from one model: ODB supports multi-database builds (static or dynamic) and generates per-database schema
Load-by-id and query-heavy workloads where statement preparation and binding overhead matter: statements are prepared once per connection and reused
Long-lived schemas: ODB has built-in schema versioning and migration, including SQLite version-aware DDL in 2.6.0
when_not_to_use: Closed-source products that cannot pay for a licence: the runtimes are GPL-2.0-only or commercial, and the Oracle and SQL Server runtimes are non-commercial-use only (NCUEL) unless you buy a licence

Toolchains without a GCC that has plugin support (gcc-N-plugin-dev): the ODB compiler is a GCC plugin, needs GCC 5 or later on the build host, and on Windows needs MinGW GCC even when the target uses MSVC
Projects that need key-value storage or an embedded engine: ODB is a mapping layer over an SQL database, not a storage engine, so it cannot compete with the key-value siblings on raw throughput
Teams that want a header-only or reflection-based library with no extra code-generation step in the build
Anyone choosing it on the Dapper comparison: on SQL Server (the database Dapper used) the author's own 2012 figures are slower than Dapper's published numbers

integration.dependencies: Build host: ODB compiler (GPL-3.0) built as a GCC plugin, needing GCC 5+ with plugin headers, libcutl and libstudxml; build2 0.18+ is the supported build system (other build systems via 'Installing ODB with build2'). Target: libodb plus libodb-sqlite (libsqlite3), libodb-pgsql (libpq), libodb-mysql (libmysqlclient or MariaDB), libodb-oracle (OCI) or libodb-mssql (SQL Server ODBC driver); optional libodb-boost, libodb-qt (Qt6 only in 2.6.0). Shared or static runtimes.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (2.6.0 dropped C++98); compiler defaults to --std c++11, std::optional mapping needs --std c++17. ODB compiler itself needs GCC 5+ with plugin support; target code can use any compiler.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (compiler via MinGW GCC; the manifest excludes non-GCC Windows builds of the compiler and static compiler builds); libodb-mysql and libodb-pgsql are excluded from wasm builds
integration.thread_safety: The connection pool is mutex- and condition-protected and hands each requesting thread its own connection (waiting threads block when max_connections is reached); the current transaction and current session are per-thread (session.hxx). Per-connection rules (statement cache, session object cache) are in the manual, which was not reachable; not documented in the files read.

gotchas: The SQLite connection pool and new-connection factories turn on SQLite shared-cache mode (SQLITE_OPEN_SHAREDCACHE) unless the database is opened with SQLITE_OPEN_PRIVATECACHE (connection-factory.cxx). SQLite discourages shared cache, and it serialises access at table level, so pass the private-cache flag when using WAL mode.
The ODB compiler picks up the gcc found on PATH (open issue #37), and new GCC releases can break it (GCC 15 support issue #25, open gcc16 static-assertion issue #34), so pin the GCC used to run ODB.

Object pointers load lazily by default, one SELECT per pointed-to object (the N+1 problem). Direct loading of containers of pointers arrived only in 2.6.0, and the polymorphic case is still open (issue #27).

Each database::begin() heap-allocates a transaction implementation, and query parameters and pooled-connection shared_ptr control blocks are also heap-allocated. The author lists these as open ideas in issue #28 with no measurements.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the embedded-kv siblings (LMDB, LevelDB, RocksDB derivatives, NuDB, UnQLite) is an ORM. Pick ODB when the data belongs in an SQL database (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL) and you want generated, prepared-statement C++ mapping code. Pick a sibling such as LMDB or LevelDB when you need a fast byte-level key-value engine and can write your own serialisation.
verified_claims_summary: The author ported Dapper's test to C++ (load 500 random Stack Overflow-style post objects one at a time). ODB 1.x on MySQL 5.1.49 under Linux (Xeon E5520 2.27 GHz per snippets) took 24 ms per 500 loads, against Dapper's own published 47 ms for hand-coded SqlDataReader and 49 ms for Dapper on SQL Server, on hardware Dapper did not state. The same author's January 2012 ODB 1.8.0 post ran ODB against SQL Server on Windows and got 222 ms (Windows 7) and 152 ms (Windows Server 2008 R2) per 500 objects; a February 2012 update gave 130 us per object locally, about 65 ms per 500 (derived). Those same-database figures are all slower than Dapper's 49 ms, so the 2x comes from comparing MySQL with SQL Server, not ODB with Dapper (search snippets only; codesynthesis.com was unreachable, and no benchmark source, compiler or flags were found).
status_note: Actively maintained by Code Synthesis: 2.6.0 was released on 2026-07-27, the issue tracker is active, and the package manifests name git.codesynthesis.com as the source repository. Usability is mixed because of the GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0/NCUEL-or-commercial licence split, and the only performance evidence is first-party 2011-2012 blog numbers that do not survive a same-database comparison.
